name: minimodem
why: Turns text into FSK modem tones and back again, a delightful transform you can hear over a speaker.

brief.what_it_is: Minimodem is a command-line program for Linux that decodes or generates audio FSK modem tones at any chosen baud rate, using various framing protocols. It can play and capture tones in real time through the system audio device, or process audio files in batch mode. It includes support for standard FSK protocols such as Bell103, Bell202, RTTY, TTY/TDD, NOAA SAME, and Caller-ID. Text or data goes in and comes out as tones you can hear, or audio goes in and text or data comes out.
brief.why_it_exists: The author presents it as a general-purpose software FSK modem for moving data between computers over an audio path, such as an audio cable, sound waves, radio, or telephone. The README praises the Unix philosophy of simple tools that do one job.
brief.how_it_works: The README does not explain the signal processing in detail. It says minimodem decodes or generates FSK tones at a specified baud rate, with framing protocols layered on top, and that it works in real time via the system audio device or in batch mode on audio files.

brief.install_notes: On Debian, Ubuntu, and Fedora it installs from the distro package manager (Ubuntu needs the kamalmostafa/minimodem PPA first). Source is on GitHub (kamalmostafa/minimodem), and a tarball minimodem-0.24.tar.gz is offered. It is a GNU/Linux program, and the README mentions a system audio device, so a working sound card or audio cable is needed for real-time use. No runtime or account setup is described. Note: the homepage gives no Homebrew-specific instructions, and the brew formula's executable is minimodem.
brief.standout: It turns an ordinary audio channel, including a speaker and microphone, into a plain data pipe with classic 1980s-era modem standards such as Bell 103 and Bell 202 available as one command. The README also lists real-world uses, such as a Sega Saturn save-game extractor and decoding Arduino output, which shows people use it for audio forensics and retro hacks as well as serious comms.
brief.status: Quiet, with some evidence of maintenance. The homepage lists source tarball 0.24 and copyright dates run 2011-2020. I could not see a release date or last-commit date on either page, so I cannot confirm recent activity.
brief.caveats: The homepage and GitHub README are thin on usage: no example commands, no flag reference, and no description of the decoder's error handling. Platform is GNU/Linux as stated; I saw no macOS notes, so the Homebrew formula may be less tested there. Licensed GPLv3 or later. The README says 'It acts a general-purpose' (a typo for 'acts as'), so treat the text as informal. Real-world results depend on audio levels and noise.

judge.reason: Minimodem turns ordinary audio into a data channel using classic modem protocols—a surprising, hands-on way to explore how information travels through sound.

entry.title: minimodem
entry.tldr: A command-line software modem that turns text into audible FSK tones and decodes them back, using classic standards like Bell 103 and Bell 202.
entry.deeper_look:
Minimodem generates or decodes audio frequency-shift keying (FSK) tones at a baud rate you choose, with framing protocols layered on top. It can work in real time through the system audio device, or in batch mode on audio files. Text or data goes in and comes out as sound; sound goes in and text or data comes out.

The built-in protocols include Bell103, Bell202, RTTY, TTY/TDD, NOAA SAME and Caller-ID. These are the tones behind old dial-up modems, teletype machines, weather radio alerts and phone line caller display. One tool covers all of them.

The author describes it as a general-purpose software FSK modem for moving data between computers over an audio path: a cable, sound waves through air, radio, or a telephone line. The README leans on the Unix philosophy of simple tools that do one job, and a quoted user says minimodem "has all the boxes ticked."

The idea underneath is that any audio channel, even a speaker and a microphone, is a data pipe if you agree on how to encode bits as pitch. The README lists uses beyond serious comms, such as extracting Sega Saturn save games and decoding Arduino output. It also dares you to decode the modem data in a demo video yourself, with the hint to try 'pavucontrol'.
entry.install:
brew install minimodem
# Upstream targets GNU/Linux. On Debian: sudo apt-get install minimodem. Real-time use needs a working audio device (sound card, or a cable/speaker and mic).

try_this.what_happens: Prints the option summary, where you can see how baud rate and protocol are chosen.
Opens the man page, which the README points to for usage since it gives no examples.

entry.whats_unique: It packs a whole family of 1980s-era modem and teletype standards into one pipe-friendly command, and works over a plain speaker and microphone.
entry.caveats: The README has no usage examples or flag reference, upstream is documented for GNU/Linux only so Homebrew on macOS may be less tested, and results depend on audio levels and noise.
